title: The 1993 Waco Siege
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the 1993 Waco siege, beginning with the history of the Branch Davidians at Mount Carmel near Waco, Texas, and David Koresh's rise and abuses. They then describe the ATF investigation, the failed undercover operations, and the February 28, 1993 raid that led to a gunfight with four agents and six Davidians killed. The episode follows the fifty-one day FBI-led siege, the negotiations (including the milk exchanges, the Bible-manuscript deal, and the tear gas insertion), the April fire that killed Koresh and dozens of others, and the aftermath, including disputed accounts of who fired first and who started the fire, the lack of government prosecutions, and the effect on the militia movement and the Oklahoma City bombing. The episode closes with a brief listener mail segment placeholder and a cruise promotion.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about George Michael and Wham, then frame the episode as a serious look at the Waco tragedy and lack of accountability, including the eighty-six deaths and twenty children.

segments.title: Origins of the Branch Davidians
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the Branch Davidian name predates David Koresh; Benjamin Roden started the branch in 1955 as a split from the Seventh-day Adventists. Koresh, born Vernon Wayne Howell, took over after Lois Roden's leadership and was involved in a shooting and an affair. The Mount Carmel compound near Waco had been active since 1935.

segments.title: Koresh's rise and abuses
segments.summary: Koresh was expelled from the Adventist church after a sexual assault allegation, married a fourteen-year-old member with her parents' consent, and claimed God told him to father many children. The hosts describe his troubled childhood and the sexual abuse of female members, including minors.

segments.title: How the outside world learned of the abuse
segments.summary: The Waco Tribune-Herald published articles on the abuse, and Australian program A Current Affair interviewed Koresh in 1992. The hosts note the ATF was not investigating the abuse but gun violations.

segments.title: Illegal weapons and ATF investigation trigger
segments.summary: The Davidians were accused of illegally buying, modifying, and selling machine guns and stockpiling ammunition, and of training members including children. A UPS driver's report of a delivery of grenade shells alerted federal authorities.

segments.title: Failed undercover operations
segments.summary: ATF agents posed as college students renting a house nearby, and later an agent posed as a UPS employee; both efforts were clumsy and quickly exposed. Robert Rodriguez embedded himself as a Bible study student and was known to be a federal agent but was not expelled.

segments.title: Planning the raid and the leaked surprise
segments.summary: The ATF obtained a warrant and planned a surprise raid based on faulty intelligence about the weapons and the men's whereabouts. A media cameraman and reporter tipped off the compound by stopping a Davidian mail carrier, the element of surprise was lost, and Rodriguez's call for cancellation was overridden. The hosts note budget-review motives.

segments.title: The February 28, 1993 raid and gunfight
segments.summary: Seventy-six agents arrived from Fort Hood in cattle trucks. Koresh met them at the door and said women and children were inside; shooting then erupted. Four agents and six Davidians died, and Koresh was wounded. Accounts of who fired first remain disputed, including the reported shooting of dogs.

segments.title: Koresh's wounds and the high-ground compound
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the compound's elevated position and tower, its largely wooden construction, and the religious symbolism of Koresh being shot through the wrist and side. A phone call with Officer Lynch is mentioned.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the siege segment.

segments.title: Start of the siege and early negotiations
segments.summary: The raid became a fifty-one day siege with the ATF and then the FBI surrounding the compound. Early FBI negotiations led to twenty-one children released, Koresh's promised hour-long sermon swap, and a March second setback when Koresh said God told him to wait. Milk was exchanged for proof-of-life videotapes.

segments.title: Government views, FBI division, and the criminal defense attorney
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how Janet Reno was briefed without seeing the videotapes, the FBI's conflicting negotiator and hostage rescue approaches, and a defense attorney who entered the compound. Koresh agreed to come out after finishing his manuscript interpreting Revelation, which Bible scholars Philip Arnold and James Tabor helped arrange.

segments.title: Pressure tactics: tanks, lights, and music
segments.summary: Koresh's promised exit was doubted by the FBI. The compound was surrounded by Bradley vehicles and tanks, and the FBI used sleep deprivation, bright lights, loudspeakers, and a tank crushing Koresh's Ford Ranchero on March 21, before negotiations collapsed.

segments.title: Tear gas insertion and tank breach
segments.summary: The FBI announced it was inserting tear gas, not lethal, and on April 19 used tanks to ram the building in high winds. Fire broke out about four hours later, with the compound's wood construction and blocked entrances making it spread quickly.

segments.title: Deaths in the fire and disputed causes
segments.summary: Koresh was found dead from a gunshot; Steve Schneider may have been involved, but this is unknown. Nine people escaped while seventy-five others died, including at least twenty children. The hosts discuss blunt force trauma deaths, gunshot and stab deaths, and disputes over whether the FBI or Davidians started the fire, including monitoring evidence.

segments.title: Aftermath: accountability and the militia movement
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the ATF flag raised over the compound, the lack of charges against government agents, a 1993 report critical of the ATF, and the galvanizing effect on the militia movement. Timothy McVeigh visited Waco and later carried out the Oklahoma City bombing on April 19, 1995.

segments.title: Ruby Ridge, conspiracy theories, and surviving Davidians
segments.summary: The hosts link Waco to Ruby Ridge and 1990s anti-government paranoia. They note the surviving Branch Davidians still exist as Branch Ministries at Mount Carmel, nine survivors were convicted on lesser charges, and many remain believers.

segments.title: Madonna tangent and wrap-up of Waco
segments.summary: The hosts close the Waco discussion with a tangent about Koresh having a Madonna picture and claiming God would give Madonna to him.

segments.title: Virgin Voyages cruise promotion
segments.summary: Hosts promote a live show on a Virgin Voyages cruise from New York to Bermuda in October and direct listeners to the website.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address for listener mail and note the show is a production of iHeartRadio.
